setting: The Latin Quarter, Paris, the days after the evening at the Café Musain
keepInMind: Turned out by his grandfather with thirty francs, Marius lodges with Courfeyrac at the hôtel de la Porte-Saint-Jacques. At the Café Musain his passionate defence of Napoleon was answered by Combeferre's 'To be free' and Enjolras's 'My mother is the Republic.'

returning.reminder: Marius's grandfather, a loud royalist of over ninety, who ordered him out of the house when he shouted 'Down with the Bourbons!'
M. Gillenormand's prim unmarried daughter, Marius's aunt, who keeps house for her father; she once paid Théodule to spy on Marius.

setting: Paris, the hard years after Marius leaves the hotel
keepInMind: With his clothes and watch sold and the hotel paid, Marius has a few francs left. He sent back his aunt's six hundred francs with a respectful letter and left the hotel rather than run into debt.

setting: Paris, once Marius's poverty has settled into a routine
keepInMind: Marius has known days without bread, worn a turned coat only after dark, and been admitted as a lawyer; his grandfather tore up the letter telling him so. His father's note asked him to do all the good he could to a sergeant named Thénardier, who saved the colonel's life at Waterloo.

returning.reminder: The rapacious innkeeper of Montfermeil who kept Cosette as a drudge. At Waterloo he was robbing the dead when Colonel Pontmercy, waking, took him for his rescuer. Marius knows only the rescuer, and found the inn at Montfermeil failed and its owner gone.

setting: Paris, three years after Marius left his grandfather's house
keepInMind: Marius lives by hack work on seven hundred francs a year in a fireless room of the Gorbeau house, never in debt. Beside his father's name he reveres one other: Thénardier's.

returning.reminder: The old churchwarden of Saint-Sulpice, brother of the curé of Vernon, who told Marius how his father came secretly to mass for years to watch him from behind a pillar.

setting: A portrait of M. Mabeuf, before and after 1830
keepInMind: Marius, now twenty, has only two friends: Courfeyrac and old M. Mabeuf, whose talk about the colonel at Saint-Sulpice changed his life.

setting: The Gorbeau house and Marius's walks, 1830 into 1831
keepInMind: Marius lodges in the Gorbeau hovel on the Boulevard de l'Hôpital, the same house where Valjean once hid with Cosette. Its poorest lodgers are the Jondrettes, a father, mother and two grown daughters; their son is the street boy Little Gavroche, whom his father ignores and his mother does not love.

returning.reminder: The destitute lodger at the end of the Gorbeau corridor, Little Gavroche's father, who told the portress that if anyone came asking for a Pole, an Italian or a Spaniard, it would be him.
The old woman who is portress, principal tenant and stair-sweeper of the Gorbeau house.

setting: M. Gillenormand's house in the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, 1831
keepInMind: Since Marius left, his grandfather has never once tried to see him, and the aunt's gifts of money keep coming back. Marius has no idea the old man misses him.

returning.reminder: Mademoiselle Gillenormand's favourite, a handsome lancer lieutenant and grand-nephew of the old man. She paid him to shadow Marius to Vernon, where he found the 'love affair' was a father's grave, and kept quiet about it.

setting: The Luxembourg garden, Paris; Marius at twenty
keepInMind: Marius is poor, proud and solitary, takes long walks alone, and sees almost no one but Courfeyrac and M. Mabeuf. He has been too shy, and too poor, to think about women.

setting: The same alley of the Luxembourg, on a summer morning after six months' absence
keepInMind: For a year Marius passed the same pair on the same bench: a white-haired man of about sixty and a plain, thin girl of thirteen or fourteen. Courfeyrac nicknamed them Monsieur Leblanc and Mademoiselle Lanoire. Marius liked the man and found the girl insipid.

setting: The Luxembourg, on a warm and luminous day
keepInMind: Coming back after six months, Marius found the awkward child had become a beautiful, well-dressed young woman. She glanced at him with indifference.

setting: The next day, at Marius's usual hour for the Luxembourg
keepInMind: The girl's eyes met Marius's for the first time, and something flashed in them. That evening he noticed how shabby the clothes he walked in had become.

setting: The Gorbeau house and the Luxembourg, the days that follow
keepInMind: In his best coat and gloves Marius walked past the bench twice, blushing, then retreated to another seat. He forgot to dine and brushed his coat before bed.

setting: Marius's bench in the Luxembourg, near the end of the second week
keepInMind: For a fortnight Marius has gone every day in his new coat and watched the bench from a distance without once going near it.

setting: The Luxembourg, the month that follows
keepInMind: As she passed his bench on her father's arm, the girl looked at Marius with pensive sweetness. He is desperately in love, and knows nothing about her, not even her name.

setting: The Luxembourg, a breezy day in May
keepInMind: Marius hides behind trees to be seen by the girl and not by her father, and she answers his looks. M. Leblanc seems to have noticed. On their bench Marius found a handkerchief marked U. F. and decided she is called Ursule.

setting: The Luxembourg, some weeks later
keepInMind: Marius's love has turned to jealous madness. M. Leblanc has changed benches and sometimes comes without his daughter.

setting: No scene: Book VII, 'Patron Minette', opens with an essay
keepInMind: This chapter steps away from the story to describe the 'mines' that undermine every society, dug by thinkers from the top down to a dark bottom layer. The story is left where Marius lost the girl: M. Leblanc moved out of the Rue de l'Ouest, leaving no address.

setting: No scene: Hugo's essay on the underside of society continues
keepInMind: This chapter goes on with the digression. Hugo has described the higher mines of religion, philosophy and revolution, dug by disinterested men; now he goes down to the last one, where there is no light.

setting: The criminal underworld of Paris, 1830 to 1835
keepInMind: Hugo has called the bottom of society a cavern of appetite and ignorance, which hates everything above it and can be cured only by light. Here he names the men who ruled it.

setting: The underworld of Paris, 1830 to 1835
keepInMind: Four ruffians rule the 'third lower floor': the colossus Gueulemer, the thin, learned Babet, the masked ventriloquist Claquesous and the pomaded youth Montparnasse, who kills to dress well.

returning.reminder: The ex-convict road-mender of Montfermeil who drank with Thénardier and haunted the forest after seeing a stranger bury something there.

setting: Paris, the summer, autumn and winter after Marius lost the girl
keepInMind: The story returns to Marius after Hugo's chapters on Patron-Minette. He kept watch under the lit windows in the Rue de l'Ouest for a week until they went dark and the porter told him the gentleman had moved away.

returning.reminder: The white-haired man of the Luxembourg, Courfeyrac's 'Monsieur Leblanc'. He noticed Marius following his daughter, stared hard at him at their gate, and moved house leaving no address.
M. Leblanc's daughter, whom Marius loves without having spoken a word to her. From a handkerchief he believes her name is Ursule.

setting: The boulevard near the Gorbeau house, on Candlemas evening in February
keepInMind: Marius has searched Paris all winter for the girl without success. Once, near the Invalides, he glimpsed a white-haired workman who looked like M. Leblanc and lost him in the side streets.

returning.reminder: Marius's neighbour in the Gorbeau house, father of Little Gavroche. Marius once secretly paid the family's rent to save them from eviction, but has never spoken to any of them.
The old portress of the Gorbeau house, whom Courfeyrac nicknamed Ma'am Bougon; she was amazed to see Marius go out in his new coat every day.

setting: Marius's garret in the Gorbeau house, that night
keepInMind: Two ragged girls running from the police brushed past Marius on the boulevard and dropped a small grey packet, which he picked up and forgot in his pocket.

setting: Marius's garret, the next morning
keepInMind: The packet held four begging letters to four patrons, signed with four different names but written by the same hand on the same tobacco-smelling paper. A soft knock has just come at Marius's door.

setting: Marius's garret, just after his visitor leaves
keepInMind: The visitor was the elder Jondrette girl, half-naked and starving, with a begging letter from her father in the same hand as the four. She took the letters back, and Marius gave her his last five francs.

setting: Marius on his commode, looking through the hole in the partition
keepInMind: Marius has found a triangular hole high in the thin wall between his room and the Jondrettes' garret, and blames himself for living beside their misery for years without looking.

returning.reminder: Jondrette's wife, Little Gavroche's mother; she loves her daughters and not her son.

setting: The Jondrettes' garret, seen through the peephole
keepInMind: Marius watches a filthy, freezing garret: Jondrette in a woman's chemise writing begging letters and cursing the rich, his huge wife by a dying fire, the younger daughter silent on a pallet.

setting: The Jondrettes' garret, minutes later, waiting in the cold
keepInMind: The 'philanthropist' from the church of Saint-Jacques-du-Haut-Pas has read the letter and is coming by cab with his daughter. Jondrette has put out the fire, broken the chair and made his younger daughter smash a pane, cutting her hand.

setting: The Jondrettes' garret, as the visitors come in
keepInMind: Marius, at the peephole, has just seen who the visitors are: M. Leblanc and the girl of the Luxembourg.

setting: The stairs and boulevard outside the Gorbeau house, as the visitors leave
keepInMind: Posing as the ruined actor Fabantou, Jondrette claimed he owes sixty francs by tonight. M. Leblanc gave five francs and his greatcoat and promised to come back at six with the sixty. Jondrette twice told his wife to take a good look at him.

setting: The stairs and corridor of the Gorbeau house, a few minutes later
keepInMind: Marius ran down to follow the visitors' cab, but he had given his money to the girl and could not pay a cab of his own, so he lost them. Coming back, he saw Jondrette, wearing M. Leblanc's greatcoat, talking on the boulevard with a prowler who looked like Panchaud, alias Bigrenaille.

setting: Marius's room, with his ear to the partition
keepInMind: The elder Jondrette girl offered to do anything for Marius, and he asked her to find the address of the old gentleman and his daughter, promising her whatever she likes. Then, through the wall, he heard Jondrette say that he has recognised the visitor.

setting: Marius leaves the Gorbeau house, that same afternoon
keepInMind: Jondrette says he knew M. Leblanc eight years ago, whispered a name about the young lady that threw his wife into a rage, and boasted that his fortune is made. Leblanc is to return at six, when the house is empty, and if he will not give in, 'we'll fix him'. Jondrette went out to see some people and ordered a charcoal brazier.

setting: The police station at No. 14 Rue de Pontoise
keepInMind: On his way, Marius overheard two men sitting behind a wall in the snow discussing an 'affair' that cannot fail with the help of Patron-Minette, the gang of Babet, Gueulemer, Claquesous and Montparnasse.

setting: The snowy Rue Mouffetard quarter, about three in the afternoon
keepInMind: The inspector Marius told knows the Gorbeau house and the gang. He took Marius's passkey, gave him two loaded pistols, and told him to fire one when the crime is about to be committed, not too soon. He is Javert, the inspector who unmasked Valjean at Montreuil-sur-Mer and hunted him through Paris to the convent wall; Marius knows nothing of that.

returning.reminder: Lesgle de Meaux, the bald, cheerfully unlucky member of the A.B.C. who answered for Marius at roll-call and got himself struck off instead.

setting: Marius's dark room in the Gorbeau house, about half past five
keepInMind: Marius shadowed Jondrette as he bought a heavy cold chisel and climbed the wall in the Rue du Petit-Banquier. Back home, he glimpsed four men sitting motionless in an empty attic along his corridor. He has Javert's two pistols.

setting: Marius's room, a few minutes before six
keepInMind: Jondrette has told his family, 'The mousetrap is open. The cats are there.' Sent to search Marius's room, the elder girl looked only in his mirror and reported no one there. Both girls are now posted outside as lookouts.

setting: Marius at the peephole, as six o'clock is about to strike
keepInMind: The garret is lit by a brazier with the chisel heating in it; there are ropes and a rope ladder by the door. Madame Jondrette took Marius's two chairs without seeing him. Jondrette tested a knife, and Marius cocked his pistol.

setting: The Jondrettes' garret, just after six
keepInMind: M. Leblanc arrived calm and laid four louis on the table for the rent. His cab has been sent away, he and Jondrette sit facing each other, and Marius believes the police are waiting outside for his shot.

setting: The Jondrettes' garret, a moment later
keepInMind: Four men with blackened faces slipped in and sat on the bed behind M. Leblanc. When Leblanc valued Jondrette's 'picture by a master' at three francs, Jondrette dropped his mask and thundered, 'Do you know me?' Marius's signal to Javert is a shot into the ceiling.

setting: Outside the Gorbeau house, earlier that same evening
keepInMind: Jondrette is Thénardier, the innkeeper of Montfermeil, and he named his prisoner as the man who carried off 'the Lark' at Christmas 1823: the reader can now see that M. Leblanc is Jean Valjean and his daughter is Cosette. Marius did not know them. Hearing the name his father told him to honour, he could not fire, and tossed in the elder girl's warning note instead. Valjean burned his own arm with the red-hot chisel to show he could not be made to talk. Javert appeared in the doorway.

setting: The Boulevard de l'Hôpital and the Gorbeau house, the following night
keepInMind: Javert arrested Thénardier, his wife and the gang. He caught the younger daughter, Azelma, on watch outside; the elder, Éponine, got away. When he turned to the bound victim, the window was open and the man was gone.

returning.reminder: Little Gavroche, the merry, unloved street boy of the boulevards, son of the 'Jondrettes', which makes him a Thénardier. He comes home only every few months to 'see mamma'.

setting: No scene: Volume IV opens with the history of 1830 to 1832
keepInMind: This chapter steps away from the story to explain the Revolution of July 1830 and the two restless years after it. The story is left with the Thénardiers and their gang in prison, Valjean and Cosette gone without a trace, and Marius still not knowing who they are.

setting: No scene: Hugo's history of 1830 continues
keepInMind: Still history, not story. Hugo has explained how the Restoration fell in July 1830 by treating the nation's charter as a gift it could take back.

setting: No scene: a portrait of King Louis Philippe
keepInMind: Still history. The 'statesmen' of 1830 stopped the revolution halfway and found their man in Louis Philippe d'Orléans, crowned by the deputies and Lafayette at the Hôtel de Ville.

setting: No scene: France under Louis Philippe, up to early 1832
keepInMind: Hugo has painted Louis Philippe as a rare, decent man in a false position. Now he turns to what was pressing on the regime as 1832 began, which brings the history back toward the story.

setting: The Faubourg Saint-Antoine, towards the end of April 1832
keepInMind: Hugo has shown the July monarchy squeezed by legitimists and republicans, by social distress and by unrest abroad, and 1832 opening with the feeling that something was coming. This chapter is still history, drawn from police reports, but it ends with Paris's secret societies.

setting: A secret meeting at the Café Musain, spring 1832
keepInMind: In the faubourgs men are swearing oaths, making cartridges and hiding powder, and the secret societies of Paris are counting their members. The Friends of the A.B.C. are among them.

returning.reminder: Chief of the Friends of the A.B.C., a grave, beautiful young republican who told Marius, 'My mother is the Republic.'
The philosopher of the A.B.C., who answered Marius's praise of Napoleon with two words: 'To be free.'
A self-taught orphan workman, a fan-maker, the one man of the people among the A.B.C. students.
The A.B.C.'s drunken sceptic, who believes in nothing except Enjolras.

setting: The Gorbeau house on the night of the ambush, and the weeks that follow
keepInMind: Marius saw Javert's ambush end with the gang arrested and the victim escaped through the window. He heard Thénardier call the girl 'the Lark' and still does not know who she or her father are. His father's will binds him to help Thénardier, who is now in prison.

setting: After the Gorbeau ambush, from Javert's side and inside La Force prison
keepInMind: Marius left the Gorbeau house that night to live with Courfeyrac and avoid testifying. Every Monday he sends five borrowed francs to Thénardier in La Force. He spends his days in a lonely field by the Gobelins that someone called 'the Lark's meadow'.

returning.reminder: The youngest of Patron-Minette's four chiefs, a pretty, pomaded youth under twenty who kills to dress well.
One of Patron-Minette's troupe, among the ruffians Javert named at the Gorbeau ambush.
M. Gillenormand's former maid, who twice sent him a baby boy, named him as the father, and got him to pay for both children.

setting: M. Mabeuf's garden at Austerlitz, one dry evening
keepInMind: From La Force, Brujon sent out a note about a house with a garden gate in the Rue Plumet. It went through Magnon to Éponine, newly out of prison, and came back marked 'biscuit': nothing to be done there.

returning.reminder: Marius's old friend, the gentle churchwarden who loves only plants and old books. Ruined after 1830, he lives in a cottage at Austerlitz near the Salpêtrière with his housekeeper Mother Plutarque.

setting: The Lark's meadow, a Monday morning some days later
keepInMind: A tall, ragged girl watered M. Mabeuf's dying garden and asked only where M. Marius could be found. He sent her to the Lark's meadow.

setting: A hidden house in the Rue Plumet, Faubourg Saint-Germain
keepInMind: Éponine has offered to take Marius to the girl's address, and he made her swear not to tell her father. The story now turns to Jean Valjean and Cosette, the 'M. Leblanc' and daughter of Marius's story, last followed by the narrator when Valjean was passing as the gardener's brother at the Petit-Picpus convent.

returning.reminder: The old gardener of the Petit-Picpus convent, once saved from under his cart by M. Madeleine. He got Valjean into the convent in a coffin and passed him off as his brother, Ultime Fauchelevent.
The learned prioress of the Petit-Picpus convent, who took on Fauchelevent's 'brother' as a second gardener and his little girl as a pupil.

setting: The Rue Plumet house and Valjean's household
keepInMind: Since 1829 Valjean has rented a hidden house in the Rue Plumet, with a secret way out into the Rue de Babylone. He lives there with Cosette and an old servant, Toussaint, having left the convent so that Cosette could choose her own life.

setting: No scene: the overgrown garden of the Rue Plumet
keepInMind: This chapter steps away from the story for a meditation on the wild garden behind the gate. Cosette has the comfortable pavilion, Valjean a bare lodge at the back; he serves in the National Guard as M. Fauchelevent, and they go out only by the Rue de Babylone door.

setting: The Rue Plumet, from the time Cosette left the convent
keepInMind: The garden has been left to itself for half a century and grown into a thicket. Hugo used it to argue that nothing in nature is small and everything is bound to everything else.

returning.reminder: Cosette's mother, who sold her hair and teeth to pay for her child and died in Montreuil-sur-Mer as Javert seized Valjean at her bedside.

setting: The Rue Plumet, as Cosette grows up
keepInMind: Cosette left the convent at fourteen, plain and half-educated, adoring Valjean. She does not know her mother's name, and when she asks, he is silent.

setting: The Luxembourg, the same months, seen from Cosette's side
keepInMind: Cosette found in her mirror that she had become beautiful, and soon she was dressing as well as any woman in Paris, while Valjean watched with dread. This was the change Marius saw in the Luxembourg after six months away.

setting: The Luxembourg, seen from Valjean's side
keepInMind: The exchange of glances that troubled Marius troubled Cosette too. She steered her father toward his bench, and the two adored each other at a distance without a word.

setting: The Barrière du Maine, at dawn one October day
keepInMind: Valjean sensed Marius, set small traps for him, and after Marius followed them home to the Rue de l'Ouest and questioned the porter, stopped going to the Luxembourg. Cosette has grown pale and silent, and father and daughter suffer side by side without speaking of it.

setting: The Rue Plumet, that winter and spring
keepInMind: At dawn Valjean and Cosette watched the chain-gang pass on its way to the galleys. Valjean was petrified, and Cosette later asked him what the galleys are like. The reader has already seen, from Marius's side, how Valjean spent one February evening in the Gorbeau garret.

setting: The empty lands beyond the Salpêtrière, near M. Mabeuf's garden, one evening
keepInMind: Valjean's burned arm kept him in bed a month; Cosette nursed him, and their old closeness came back with the spring.

returning.reminder: The Thénardiers' son, the street boy who found his parents and sisters taken to prison after the Gorbeau ambush, said 'Ah!', and went off singing.
The young dandy of Patron-Minette who kills to dress well; he slipped away from the Gorbeau ambush.

setting: The Rue Plumet, April 1832
keepInMind: Since the Luxembourg walks stopped, Cosette has lost sight of Marius. Meanwhile Gavroche stole a purse back from Montparnasse after an old passer-by gave it to him, and tossed it over the hedge to M. Mabeuf.

returning.reminder: Marius's cousin, the handsome lancer lieutenant whom his aunt tried to install as a substitute grandson; M. Gillenormand ended by calling him a fool.

setting: The Rue Plumet, the first fortnight of April, with Valjean away
keepInMind: Cosette's grief over Marius is fading. She has started watching for the handsome lancer, Théodule, who passes the gate every day. Marius, meanwhile, is sinking toward despair.

setting: The stone bench by the garden railings, an evening in April
keepInMind: Cosette heard footsteps in the garden at night and saw a man's shadow in a round hat beside her own. Valjean watched for three nights and laughed it off as the shadow of a chimney-pot.

setting: The notebook Cosette found under the stone
keepInMind: A large stone appeared on Cosette's bench while she was away from it. Under it next morning she found an unaddressed envelope with a little notebook of numbered pages in a fine hand.

setting: Cosette, as she finishes reading the notebook
keepInMind: The notebook is a string of unsigned thoughts on love, on parted lovers, on a lost address and a smile under a white crape bonnet.

setting: The Rue Plumet garden, at dusk that evening
keepInMind: Cosette knew at once who wrote the notebook. The lancer now looks hideous to her, and she has fallen back in love, crediting angels with bringing the pages.

setting: The Thénardier family's history since 1823, then the streets after the Gorbeau arrests
keepInMind: Marius and Cosette met at last in her garden, kissed, and only at the end told each other their names. The story now goes back to the Thénardiers: the parents are in prison after the Gorbeau ambush, Éponine is free, and Gavroche roams the streets.

returning.reminder: M. Gillenormand's former maid, who made him pay for two little boys she said were his. Brujon's note from La Force went through her to Éponine.
Thénardier's huge, coarse wife, who loved her daughters and not her son, and threw a paving-stone at Javert at the Gorbeau house; she is in prison.

setting: The streets of Paris, a freezing, stormy spring evening in 1832
keepInMind: The Thénardiers had two more sons after 1823 and handed them to Magnon to replace her own two dead boys, so that M. Gillenormand's money would keep coming. After the police raided Magnon's house, the little boys were locked out, lost the address they had been given, and are wandering the streets. Gavroche has never known they exist.

setting: La Force prison, the same stormy night
keepInMind: Gavroche took in two lost little boys, fed them, and bedded them down inside the plaster elephant of the Bastille. Montparnasse told him Babet had escaped, and before dawn called him out to lend a hand.

returning.reminder: Patron-Minette's man in La Force since the Gorbeau ambush, who smuggled out the note about the Rue Plumet.
The colossus of Patron-Minette, a cold-blooded assassin, arrested by Javert at the Gorbeau house.

setting: No scene: Book VII, 'Slang', is an essay on argot
keepInMind: This chapter steps away from the story to defend and explore thieves' slang; the next four chapters are all essay. The story is left after the escape from La Force, where Gavroche climbed a flue and brought down his own father. The two little boys he sheltered are his brothers, though he does not know it.

setting: No scene: the essay on slang continues
keepInMind: Still a digression. Hugo has argued that slang is the language of misery itself, and that the historian of a society's depths has as serious a job as the historian of its kings and battles.

setting: No scene: the essay on slang continues
keepInMind: Still a digression. Hugo has traced slang's borrowings from a dozen languages and its three roots: invented words, metaphor, and deformed words.

setting: No scene: the last chapter of the essay on slang
keepInMind: Hugo has shown slang's songs turning from lament to insolent gaiety in the eighteenth century, a warning sign he thinks the French Revolution headed off. He now draws his conclusions.

setting: The Rue Plumet garden, May 1832
keepInMind: The story resumes after the slang chapters. Marius and Cosette met at last in her garden at dusk, kissed, and exchanged names: Marius, Cosette. Valjean knows nothing of it.

returning.reminder: The Thénardiers' elder daughter, out of prison, who promised to lead Marius to the girl's address though she plainly loves him herself. When he offered her five francs she let the coin fall.

setting: The Rue Plumet garden, May 1832, while cholera ravages Paris
keepInMind: Marius slips in every evening through a loose bar in the gate. Their love is chaste: one first kiss, hands held, nonsense talked. Cosette has told him her real name is Euphrasie.

setting: The Rue Plumet household, the same weeks
keepInMind: Marius and Cosette have told each other almost nothing beyond their names. He has never mentioned the Gorbeau ambush or her father's strange flight from it.

setting: The Rue Plumet at nightfall, 3 June 1832
keepInMind: Courfeyrac noticed Marius coming home at one in the morning but could not get a name out of him. One evening, at the corner of the Rue Plumet, Éponine stopped Marius; he answered awkwardly, and she left without finding words.

returning.reminder: Éponine's father, the former innkeeper of Montfermeil, who escaped from La Force over the wall on the night Gavroche climbed up with the rope.

setting: The Rue Plumet, after the ruffians leave
keepInMind: Éponine sat guard beside the loose bar and faced down six robbers, her own father among them, threatening to scream and bring the police until they withdrew.

setting: Inside the Rue Plumet garden, that same evening
keepInMind: While Éponine held the gate and the gang gave way to her, Marius was in the garden with Cosette. Hugo now goes back to the two of them.

setting: M. Gillenormand's house in the Rue des Filles-du-Calvaire, the next day
keepInMind: Valjean has told Cosette to be ready to travel, perhaps to England, within the week. Penniless, Marius swore he will die if she goes, said he would 'try something', and scratched his address, 16 Rue de la Verrerie, on the garden wall.

returning.reminder: Marius's grandfather, now past ninety-one, who drove him out four years ago over his father and has secretly pined for him ever since.
Marius's prim aunt, who keeps her father's house and kept sending Marius money he returned.

setting: The Champ-de-Mars, about four in the afternoon of the same day
keepInMind: Marius asked his grandfather's leave to marry Mademoiselle Fauchelevent. The old man softened, then assumed she was a lancer's conquest and advised him to make her his mistress. Marius said farewell and left, and M. Gillenormand collapsed calling his name.

setting: Marius's wanderings after leaving his grandfather
keepInMind: Valjean has resolved on England because he has seen Thénardier prowling the quarter. That morning he found '16 Rue de la Verrerie' scratched on his garden wall, and on the Champ-de-Mars a figure in a grey blouse dropped a note on his knees: 'Move away from your house.'

setting: M. Mabeuf's cottage at Austerlitz, the spring of 1832
keepInMind: Marius took Javert's two pistols, wandered for a night and a day, and on the evening of 5 June found Cosette's house shut and empty. Resolved to die, he heard a voice he half knew call through the trees that his friends were waiting at the barricade of the Rue de la Chanvrerie.

returning.reminder: Marius's old friend the botanist, growing poorer by the month at Austerlitz with his housekeeper Mother Plutarque. A purse dropped over his hedge one night; Gavroche threw it.

setting: No scene: Book X, 'The 5th of June, 1832', opens with an essay
keepInMind: This chapter steps away from the story to ask what a revolt is made of. The story stands on 5 June 1832: fighting has broken out in Paris, Marius is heading for a barricade with Javert's pistols, and old Mabeuf, who has sold his last book, has walked out toward the shooting.

setting: No scene: Hugo's essay on revolt continues
keepInMind: Hugo has set out the cautious 'golden mean' case against riots, that they cost money, hurt trade and end in massacres, and rejected it for looking only at effects. Now he looks for causes.

setting: Paris, spring 1832, up to the funeral of General Lamarque on 5 June
keepInMind: Hugo has distinguished insurrection, the whole nation rising against a usurping part, from revolt, a part attacking the whole. He has promised to tell one little-known episode of 5 and 6 June 1832 that he saw himself. Cholera has hung over Paris for three months.

setting: Paris, the afternoon of 5 June 1832
keepInMind: General Lamarque's funeral crossed an armed, agitated Paris. At the Austerlitz bridge a horseman raised a red flag, dragoons met the crowd, shots were fired, and the riot exploded.

setting: Paris away from the fighting, the evening of 5 June
keepInMind: Within hours barricades rose at twenty points, armourers' shops were looted, and by five o'clock a third of Paris was in the insurgents' hands. As night fell the government hesitated and the tocsin of Saint-Merry began to ring.

setting: The boulevards, as Lamarque's funeral crowd scatters, 5 June
keepInMind: The history chapters end here, and Hugo follows his own characters into the riot.

returning.reminder: Thénardier's son, the street boy who sheltered two lost little boys in the elephant of the Bastille and climbed the La Force wall to free his father. He does not know the boys are his brothers.

setting: The Marais, Gavroche on the march
keepInMind: Gavroche borrowed an old holster-pistol from a junk shop and set off for the fighting singing, then found it has no trigger.
